answer: The cost of tenant turnover adds up fast: lost rent, cleaning and repairs, advertising and any concession. With rents easing and new buildings opening, Winnipeg renters can shop around, so keeping a good tenant is often the cheaper choice. In a Winnipeg winter, windows and doors are among the upgrades tenants feel every day.

blocks.x: The market has tilted toward renters

Two trends are giving tenants more choice, and that makes the cost of tenant turnover worth working out. First, rents are softening: [liv.rent's October 2026 report](https://liv.rent/blog/?p=69631) puts the average unfurnished one-bedroom asking rent at $1,319, down three months in a row from a July peak of $1,353.

Second, supply is growing: [City of Winnipeg figures](https://www.winnipeg.ca/news/2026-08-20-winnipeg-leads-major-canadian-cities-housing-growth) show housing completions up 52.7% in the first seven months of 2026. Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation's most recent annual survey put Winnipeg's purpose-built rental vacancy rate at [2.8% in October 2025](https://www.gov.mb.ca/cca/rtb/resource_list/noticetomove.pdf), and [its report](https://eppd1strscr01.blob.core.windows.net/cmhcprdcontainer/sf/project/archive/housing_markets/rentalmarketreportcanadaandselectedmarkets/rental-market-report-2025-fall-en.pdf) says more vacant options drove turnover.
For landlords, losing a good tenant is harder to absorb when the next one has more options.
The cost of tenant turnover: the retention math

There is no honest single figure for what a turnover costs, because it depends on your rent, how long the unit sits empty and what it needs. Fill in this worksheet with the numbers from your last turnover:

head: Turnover cost
What to fill in
rows: Monthly rent divided by 30, times the days the unit sat empty
What you paid to get the unit ready
Listing fees, plus staff hours times what those hours cost you
Concession to re-lease in a softer market
Any free rent or discount you gave to fill the unit

blocks.x: As a reference point, at liv.rent's $1,319 average, one empty month is $1,319 in lost rent before anything else on the list. Add the other lines, and one turnover can reach thousands of dollars.
Then compare your total with a written quote for the upgrade you have in mind. Spending on something a tenant values, and keeping them another two years, can be the better trade.
Our view: comfort beats cosmetics for retention

Cold rooms, fogged windows, drafty doors and outside noise are things tenants live with every day. Those are comfort problems, and in Winnipeg the cold-weather ones peak from November to March, ahead of any spring renewals.

That is why [window and door installations](/services/windows-and-doors) deserve a bigger place in [retention planning](/blog/tenant-retention-upgrades-lease-renewal). A new window or entry door is something tenants notice every day. It can reduce drafts and condensation, cut outside noise and make a unit feel brighter. It also protects the building, because failing windows can let in water that damages walls and floors.
Where to start
Not every window needs replacing. A practical approach:
**Ask tenants.** A short survey or maintenance log will show which units complain about cold, drafts or condensation.
**Inspect the worst units first.** Look for failed seals (fogging between panes), rotted frames, gaps around trim and doors that do not latch or seal.
**Prioritize by exposure.** North- and west-facing units and ground-floor entries tend to suffer most in winter.
**Bundle work.** Replacing windows building-wide, or by elevation, can lower the per-unit cost compared with one-off replacements.
**Schedule with tenants.** Agree on access dates ahead of time, and ask your contractor to put the schedule in writing.

In a building built or renovated before 1990, check for asbestos before old caulking, putty or plaster around the frames is disturbed. Our guide covers [asbestos testing before you renovate](/blog/asbestos-testing-before-renovating-manitoba).
Don't forget the main entrance

Building entry doors and vestibules shape tenants' and visitors' first impression every day. A main door that sticks, slams, or lets snow blow in tells residents the building is not maintained. Replacing it is a contained project that can do a lot for how a building feels.
The energy angle

Manitoba Hydro's path is a 4.0% general rate increase in 2026, then [electricity revenue increases](https://www.pubmanitoba.ca/v1/contact-us/media/pubs/2026-nr/nr-mh-gra-fiscal-2026-2028-march-19-2026-english.pdf) averaging 3.5% in 2027 and 3.0% in 2028. Your class may differ. In buildings where the landlord pays for electric heat, tighter windows and doors can also cut operating costs. Where tenants pay, lower bills are another reason to stay.

[Efficiency Manitoba's rebate of $100 per qualifying window or door](https://efficiencymb.ca/my-home/windows-and-doors-rebate/) is for a primary residence, including a tenant's, and apartments are not eligible. Apartment buildings may qualify through its [Building Envelope Program](https://efficiencymb.ca/business/building-envelope/) instead.
Making the case to owners

Property managers often need to justify window and door spending to owners who see it as a cost with no rent increase attached. The retention math above is the strongest argument. Track turnover costs for a year, including vacancy, repairs, advertising and concessions.

Then compare them with the cost of the upgrades that address the reasons your tenants give for leaving. Add the reduction in repeat work orders for drafty windows and sticking doors, and the reduced risk of water damage from failed openings.
That combination of fewer turnovers, fewer repairs and lower risk can make a strong case for envelope upgrades in an older building, even with no change in rent.
The bottom line
When renters have options, landlords compete on experience. Comfortable, quiet, draft-free units help keep tenants, and in Winnipeg windows and doors are where that comfort starts.
